n101.text: Last time, we learnt that a magnet is usually made of iron or steel, and it attracts the steel pin. But it ignored the copper wire, and copper is a metal!

n201b.text: We rinsed two empty cans for recycling.

n202.text: A little snail is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

n203b.text: Look low, where it is wet!

n204.text: Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

n401.text: Round one. Which can will the magnet pull? One, the drink can. Two, the food tin. Three, both. Show me your fingers.

n403m.text: Three! They are both metal cans, and they are both shiny and silver.

n404p.text: Two. At home, a fridge magnet held on to a food tin like this. I tested it.

n405b.text: Two! Dad says drink cans like this are made of aluminium. And aluminium is not iron or steel!

n501.text: Be an aluminium can! Shrink down. Quietly.

n502.text: You are an empty drink can, made of aluminium. Clunk! You drop into the blue recycling bin.

n503.text: A truck takes you to a recycling plant. You ride a moving belt, with steel food tins and plastic bottles.

n504.text: Above the belt hangs a giant magnet. Clang! The steel tins jump up onto it.

n505.text: But you roll right on. The magnet does not pull you, even though you are a metal.

n601.text: The answer is two: the steel food tin! Did you show two fingers? Put one finger up!

n701m.text: But the drink can and the copper wire are both metal. Why does the magnet ignore them?

n702.text: Look closer. Basil's magnet passes every object on our table, and not one of them moves.

n703.text: These objects are made of non-magnetic materials.

n704b.text: Non means not. Non-magnetic materials are the ones a magnet does not attract, like wood, glass and plastic!

n705p.text: Here is the surprise. Copper and aluminium are metals, but they are non-magnetic too!

n706m.text: So being a metal is not enough! Only some metals, like iron and steel, are magnetic.

n709.text: Objects that are not attracted to magnets are made of non-magnetic materials. Non-magnetic materials include ceramic, fabric, glass, plastic, rubber and wood. Metals such as aluminium and copper are also non-magnetic.

n801.text: Showdown! Double points. Basil's homework has one mistake. Line one, two, or three? Show me with your fingers.

n802b.text: One: the iron nail is attracted, so it is magnetic. Two: the wooden ruler is not attracted, so it is non-magnetic. Three: the foil is shiny and grey, like steel, so it is magnetic.

n804m.text: Three! We cannot tell by looking. The magnet did not attract the foil, so the foil is non-magnetic.

n805.text: Three fingers? Put up two more on your score hand!

n901.text: Our new theme is called Interactions. When you push a swing, it moves away from you.

n902.text: Magnets interact with other objects too.

n903p.text: Interact means one thing acts on another. The magnet pulls the pin, and the pin moves!

n904.text: Look closer. Bring the magnet near each object, and watch how they interact.

n905.text: One of the ways to classify these materials is to observe how they interact with a magnet.

n906m.text: To classify is to sort things into groups. The magnet sorts them into two groups: magnetic and non-magnetic!

n908.text: A magnet can interact with objects that are made of magnetic materials.

c1003.text: Iron and steel? Magnetic! Copper and aluminium? Non-magnetic! Do not guess! Test it with a magnet!

n1101.text: Show me your score hand! More than one? You beat the Buddies. Three fingers? High five!

n1102.text: Did you spot the snail? It was on a wet leaf of the potted plant!

n1103b.text: Here is a fun fact! Deep in the sea lives a snail with iron in its shell. A magnet can attract this snail!

n1201.text: Next time: two ring magnets on a pencil! The top one floats in mid-air, with no glue and no string. What holds it up? One, a pull. Two, a push. Lock in your answer!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?
